items.body:
Forever Records presents an extensive reissue edition of the first 'fully released' Psychick Warriors Ov Gaia album.

"Dancing on the wildest edge of the 90s outsider techno zeitgeist while proudly independent of any so-called scene, Ov Biospheres And Sacred Grooves: A Document Ov New Edge Folk Classics is both of its time and out of time. Rooted in the experiments of electronic music pioneers, industrial culture and ethnic music from around the globe while responding to the house and techno explosion, Robbert Heynen, Reinier Brekelmans, Reinoud van den Broek and Tim Freeman's freewheeling masterpiece takes in lush electronica and murky abstraction on its singular voyage through parts unknown.

Originally released in 1992, this is the first time the full, previously CD-only, version of Ov Biospheres and Sacred Grooves will be pressed on vinyl. The original LP and CD artwork from the various editions released in the early 90s has been combined and designed by the band, and the audio has been remastered with their full approval. 

Forever Records is a reissue series dedicated to rediscovering lost musical treasures from across the spectrum of head-feeding, heart-rending electronic music. Established by Rush Hour co-founder Christiaan Macdonald and Delsin founder Marsel van der Wielen, Forever Records places heartfelt faith in a carefully curated sequence of seminal, largely forgotten records from disparate eras, scenes and spaces within electronic music history. Tipped towards the mellow and introspective, these are albums that stop time when the needle hits the groove, stirring only when it's time to flip over before you sink back into the experience. That's what albums were always meant to be about, back then, right now, always and forever."

Mesmerising, illuminated sound environments conjured by Werner Durand, a key foil of CC Hennix & Amelia Cuni, joined by his Cuni spar Uli Hohmann on Mid-Eastern drums, Tibetan bells, and electronics on three intrepid, rhythmic drone excursions calling to mind Michael Ranta, Robert Rutman, Jon Hassell.

"WERNER DURAND has made himself a name with various projects with Dhrupad singerAMELIA CUNI, playing with URBAN SAX, ARNOLD DREYBLATT, HENNING CHRISTIANSEN, DAVID BEHRMAN, ELLEN FULLMAN, CATHERINE CHRISTER HENNIX, as the co-founder of THE 13th TRIBE, ARMCHAIR TRAVELLER and TONALIENS (with ROBIN HAYWARD and HILARY JEFFERY) plus numerous solo albums, released on labels like Black Truffle, Unseen Worlds or Edition Telemark. Having studied saxophone as well as Indian / Persian flutes, the Berlin based DURAND is a highly reputated protagonist in the drone scene, famous for his self-built wind instruments like buzz-clarinets or his PVC neys & horns.

His partner in FLOCKS (and longtime personal friend) is ULI HOHMANN whose early encounters with music from Asia, India and Africa led to studies with the Ghanaian master drummer MUSTAPHA TETTEY ADDY and later Tombak and Daf with NEMAD DARMAN (Iran). HOHMANN played in a couple of projects that explored the language of classical Persian music, and started building his own stringed instruments (being an educated carpenter). In 2014 he joined DURAND and AMELIA CUNI for the album "Clearing", and 2018 DURAND and HOHMANN decided to continue as a duo: FLOCKS was born.

On "Lagoon", the duo further explores the aesthetics it has crafted on its selftitled debut (2023, on the now defunct ZEHRA imprint): DURAND and HOHMANN shape drone-y soundscapes based on their self-built wind- & stringed instruments, Persian percussion and subtle electronics, drawing additional inspiration from Krautrock (listen to the irresistible, hypnotique, ever-changing rhythmic pattern of the title track) as well as JON HASSELL's "fourth world" aesthetics, placing the duo nicely between tradition and experiment!"

items.body:
The roots of so much modern groove-driven music are reflected in Soundway’s study of rare jazz, calypso and drum music from ‘70s Trinidad & Tobago, the Caribbean nation off the coast of Venezuela.

In that time between artists first plugging in their instruments, and computerising them, the psychedelic sheen and sonification of US & UK pop and dance musics would also rub off on modernisers in the Caribbean. Under the Trinidadian term for calypso, “kaiso” the artists showcased here would blend Afro-American and West Indian traditions with certain studio innovations from disco and psych-rock to a clear purpose: driving dances - and everything that comes with them - in their lush isles.

The results are hip-gripping, heat-seeking gems that factor Black Atlantic links for a new, independent era un-tethered from colonial influence, ranging from the deeply soul-stirring jazz hush and rumble of ‘Ogun’ by Clive Zanda, thru Abdul Malik de Coteau’s plangent lament set to air-rippling steel drums, taking in the spiritual Latin jazz of Michael Boothman’s ‘Tabu’ brimming with optimism, to the muy caliente calypso of Andre Tanker, heads-down drum vibrations of Mansa Musa, and psych-funk fusioneering of Frends on ‘Mystery Music’.

items.body:
Following records on Quiet Time and Miami's Schematic, Cairo-based producer Mostafa Onsy arrives on the mighty Drowned By Locals with a unique adaptation of 808 Mafia's iconic trap sound that pulls in influences from classic '90s Egyptian pop and mahraganat.

'Baba Fen' might come as a surprise if you've heard Onsy's previous records, like 2021's dark, trippy IDM suite 'MetaConc' and its predecessor, a nostalgia trip that took its blueprint from AFX's '90s gear. Here, the producer takes his cues from Southside, TM88 and Lex Luger's iconic Atlanta trap productions: the ratcheting hi-hats, overdriven 808 kicks and acidic trance risers that characterized American music in the wake of breakouts from Future. Honestly, it works - we've long maintained the similarities between IDM's skittering beats and trap's, and Onsy's a natural, dropping a familiar ATL snare and FL Studio synths between mahraganat hand drums and those ubiquitous pitched hi-hat runs on the scene-setting 'Zabet Ekaa3 (Intro)'.

He's joined by local vocalists Fara7 and Bleng on 'Fnan', who help assert the album's Egyptian relevance, draping their melancholy AutoTuned slurs and ad-libs around Onsy's clever fusion of half-speed local percussion and trap's signature soundset. And the two MCs are joined by gravelly-voiced rapper Sakt on the album's brilliant title track, where Onsy supplies his spookies FM-laced beats, phonk-adjacent slaps that wouldn't be out of place on one of Raider Klan's early mixtapes. Rubber-voiced Drowned By Locals regular illfeel shows up on 'Fantanyel' and goes toe-to-toe with Bleng on 'Blikii', trading blows over one of Onsy's most ominous productions. Recommended.

Polish performance artist, musician, and poet Wojciech Kosma spills the contents of his heart on 'Tajemnica', a postmodern pop deconstruction that's between David Sylvian and Yung Lean.

There's a confusing quality to 'Tajemnica' that makes it difficult to engage with at first. It's produced almost ineptly, made with demo-like sounds that create a haze of preset nostalgia around Kosma's voice. It's only after a few tracks that the sound rights itself, and Kosma's intention makes itself clear. The record couldn't be any other way; the minimalism of the production just makes his voice stand out even more. Listen to the ominous 'Skrzydła', where a beat barely scratches the surface of Kosma's light synths - it's left to his lyrics, in Polish of course, to do the heavy lifting. And when different club sounds are referenced, it's inevitably oblique - a dancehall beat here, a log drum there. The sketchiness makes it sound like pop music that's been plucked out of a brain scanner, not completely whole, but not inhuman either.

This is pure class! Bobby Ingham’s darkly cinematic debut LP seriously strikes a nerve for admirers of Space Afrika, Mark Leckey, Burial & Low End Activist with its evocation of life in C.21st West Yorkshire manifest in a tensely paranoid, homesick patch-work of knifed samples wrapped up in weightless grime & UKG structures

‘Angel Of The North’ inarguably hits a high water mark of Sneaker Social Club’s retro-futurist UK fixations with a deeply impressive demonstration of sound design tekkerz at the service of immersive, narrative-driven impressionism. For 30 mins the 24 year old Ingham belies his yung years with a grasp of melancholic pathos, atmospheric subtlety and articulate crud that one may expect from an artist years his senior. He effectively has us rapt front to back, from the frisson of noctilucent pads and dread subs in ‘Lynne’ to the lush resolution of ‘I Can’t Believe It’, hustling listeners heavy into what the label term a “social-realist inversion of sound system music that relishes negative space while telling a street-level story.”

That story is most suggestively limned via judicious sampling from a mix of personal and public archives, diffused across a spectra of ghostly, ephemeral arrangements perfused with flashes of the music he grew up with; from snatches of Wonder & T2 in the chamber grime abstract ‘Easy Mush’, thru skipping UKG reduced to Burial-esque degrees on ‘WYD Tomorrow Night.’ But it’s the poetic sense of restraint and sensuality that practically makes it a spiritual successor to label boss Low End Activist’s own evocation of life growing up on Oxford council estates (‘Hostile Utopia’ & ‘Municipal Dreams’), and clearly comparable to Mark Leckey’s collaged art-film soundtracks as much as the northern romanticism of Space Afrika’s liminal ambiance, or even EXLRUTH’s chamber adaptations of makina in its dare-to-differ approach and spellbinding effect. 

Big tip!

items.body:
A Detroit house/jazz masterpiece, 2004, mercifully back in circulation on vinyl for as long as stocks last (ie, not long) - don’t think twice if you spent the last 20 years kicking yourself for missing out - really is the GOAT.

'Black Mahogani’ first landed some 10 years into Kenny Dixon Jr.’s catalogue and firmly pinned him on the map with its hugely ambitious scope and attention to detail. His 5th and arguably most celebrated studio album, it’s also by far his most coveted, partly due to being neglected from reissue schemes, which has led to a status that’s grown in step with KDJ’s renown. 

It still fully kills with ten top shelf cuts sifted from prized 12”s dating back to the late ‘90s and here stitched with exclusive gear into a sort of deep jazz soundtrack updated with a Detroit house heartbeat and leagues-deep soul, effortlessly bridging epochs with timeless steez.

To pluck a few jewels from its crown, centrepiece ’Shades of Jae’ is a masterclass in deferred kick drum gratification that never fails in the dance, and the lush, jazz-taught sashay of ‘Runaway’ and sampledelia of ‘Mahogani 9000’ still take our breath away. But it’s really all best taken in longform context, from the first frisson of hi-hats and Roberta Sweed’s aching croon on ‘Holiday’ thru the filter chicanery of a closing title tune that only sets one up to do it over and again...

Aged well this one, Steven Hitchell aka Echospace aka Intrusion with set of analogue dubs very much in the spirit of Rhythm & Sound, including a strong contribution from Paul St. Hilaire aka Tikiman just to complete the act of worship. Now 15 years since it was last in circulation, the album has been remastered and is available as a double LP for the first time ever.

The Deepchord/Echospace axis is definitely having a moment. After a period where it was dismissed by some as a sort of unnecessary facsimile of Mark & Moritz’s OG blueprint, the benefit of hindsight has marked Hitchell and Modell’s productions as very much their own thing, still indebted to Berlin, but with their own signature. 

Perhaps it’s the analogue production that lends the material an air of slightly uncontrolled brilliance; the hiss of the mixing desk feels tangible rather than just digital decoration - less cosplay, more weighty and propulsive.

However - be in no doubt - if you’ve a love for anything on the line from Basic Channel to M-Series, Main Street, Burial Mix, Rhythm & Sound and Chain Reaction, this stuff is absolutely your next port of call - and this one here is one of the best from the label too, just check the clips and you’ll know exactly where you are.

Graduate of Mahogani Music and Databass, Detroit’s Sheefy McFly hits critical jit x juke x ghetto-tech x footwork momentum on six vocal bangers for Amsterdam’s Cape St. Francis. Big one FFO Hi-Tech, Omar-S, Urban Tribe, DJ Assault

Known to 313 locals for his colourful murals all over the city, and on this sleeve, Sheefy McFly also trades in a mean vein of uptempo booty music, as heard at his Ghettotechtopia parties and recently on a self-released LP and an ode to local ghetto-tech hotspot, ‘Belle Isle 2099’. His ‘Baddies Only’ EP elevates a signature sound of scudding 808 bass, claps, and keys with a spotlight on six original vocalists from his ends, each characteristic of classic-contemporary Motor City club music and its bridges to Chicago ghettotech.

From the front, he loops bars by duo Etherpussy on undulating subs and electrosoul chords in a style shared by Lola Damone’s bars on ‘Pretty World’, and also calling to mind Andrés’ class GT Flips - a reference point for the choppier soul of ‘You’re Mine’, which tilts more into footwork angularity. Tiptonaires also brings a fierce but warm energy with her faux naïf bars on the chromatic synths of ‘Cute2Nite’, while your trunk’s Cerwin Vegas get a proper test in the Miami Bass-type tremors of ‘Young N Turnt’, voiced by DJ Mobetta.

Party guaranteed!

Recorded straight to tape in Glasgow, poet/performer Lisa Jones and VOM's Chas Lalli's Gilchard debut is refreshingly human, a grotesque blend of ugly reality and absurdity that situates itself between Electrelane, Arab Strap, Dry Cleaning and early Factory biz.

'Chins for Lefty' might be Gilchard's first recording, but Jones and Lalli are hardly newcomers. Since the mid-'00s, Lalli has been a member of Glaswegian post-punk/noise rock trio VOM, moonlighting in Bad Aura and the art-punk outfit Dragged Up, where he first collided with Jones. A writer and poet with a background in the local spoken word/improv scene, Jones' lyrics provide the backbone for Gilchard's sound, building a surreal parallel Glasgow that Lalli meets head-on with jangling guitars, frazzled drum loops and murky synths. Even the recording process itself plays a part, lending the album a timeless quality - honestly if you assured us this was an excavated private press gem from the late '80s we'd probably believe you.

"I turn your picture to face the wall," Jones deadpans on 'Posthumous Hologram', breaking her monotone to sing a real chorus while Lalli stacks organ vamps and Vini Reilly guitars in the space beneath. And the duo decelerate their sound significantly on 'Break Up with Johnny Dogbirth', sounding as heroin-addled as The Velvet Underground as they work in slow motion, batting emotional reflections to each other over an almost inaudible drum beat.

items.body:
After slaying with her cold fusions of ’90s R&B, ’00s brukfunk and footwork on 2024’s ‘Concentrate’ EP and last year’s ‘Come Alive’ album, NZO returns with a deadly hyper-jiggy session for DDS - huge one FFO Various Production, Beatrice Dillon, Dolo Percussion, Rian Treanor, Akufen, El-B.

Captured at Rotherham Minster (the finest perpendicular church in Yorkshire, don’t u know) for SoYo’s annual electronics music showdown, No Bounds, NZO’s custom-built results brim with an unusual grasp of the funk, prompting a uniquely jittery rush offset with a wicked refusal of rhythmic anticipation that does crazy things with your limbs. With the finest grasp of ghost snares and the confidence to slap and tickle drums where others wouldn’t, she deftly dances thru fresh routes of rhythmic pursuit. Low-key, this sort of experimental ingenuity betrays her background in the sciences, as much as a keen ear for offbeat and upfront dance musics -  effortlessly joining and short-circuiting oblique dots between Timbaland x The Neptunes’ rugged nuance, El-B’s whipsmart torsion, RP Boo’s legwork and Beatrice Dillon’s precision-tooled arrangements, all gelled with daring confidence in her own thing. 

We can't tell you if NZO's a DJ or nah, but she approaches her set with a serious understanding of how to take control of your limbs, linking rhythms, samples and melodic phrases as if she's grandstanding on four CDJs. She rushes towards euphoria with truncated R&B coos that she expertly threads between dub stabs and garage-y organ vamps, keeping the jerky rhythms intact throughout. And just when you think you've tapped in, sugar-sweet vocals and brassy fanfares cut into a shudder of drums, an 'ANTI EP'-era AE bass whoosh comes out of nowhere to remind you where you are. 

NZO patches together an authentically Yorkshire-coded reaction to New York's post-GHE20G0TH1K evolution, the self-consciously p2p-driven movement that helped shape visionary DJs like Total Freedom and Juliana Huxtable. But she’s less conspicuously "deconstructed" than her predecessors and champions Sheffield's avant history, referencing Warp's early run, Mark Fell's continuous influence and the perpetual grind of heavy industry, blending these elements with her spectrum of influences from further afield. Freaky, hyper-articulated movers need to check it at the nearest opportunity, trust.

Luke Slater’s pioneering bleep techno vessel PAS returns to a club landscape that he helped spawn in the ’90s, with a striking exposition of techno purism primed for the new wave of pouting pumpers.

Beamed in direct from his Space Station Ø studio for longtime patrons Ostgut Ton, ‘Planetary People’ trades in a patented style of machine music that Slater, along with Detroit legends such as Jeff Mills, Claude Young, and Terrence Dixon, plus European heads Donato Dozzy or Steve Bicknell, have made into the the prevailing sound of Berlin and contemporary techno clubs worldwide. 

Slater’s feel for effortless momentum continues to make his work stand out from the crowd on these 13 new missives, each eagerly awaiting application in warehouse endurance tests and late-for-work crosstown trots. As such it rolls out in thru-line for those who consume albums as intended, with expert harness and whip control from the acid afterburn of intro ‘Into the Night’ to what sounds like Konono No.1 at Berghain in ‘Labyrinth’, peak time canter in ‘Thunder Major’, and 9 minutes of sublime tension to closer ‘Presently My Soul Grew Stronger’.

But if you just need to big rockets, ‘Quadrant 10’ will electrify any ‘floor with its rattling buzz, and the tight knit arps of ‘Brave Cosmo’ will piston tendons along with the cavernous slay of ‘Retina Burn’, and you just know the recoiling bounce of ‘Beton Brut’ is going to soundtrack some of the heaviest club and festival moments of summer ’26 and beyond.

items.body:
Bruce remixes Quade's 2025 LP 'The Foel Tower' on a limited cassette for his Poorly Knit label.

"Back in 2023, Bruce was approached by a band of young and ambitious lads, who wanted him to mix their debut album 'Nacre'. Being fans of his music, they hoped to utilise his renowned, club-informed and emotive sound design to add a shade of hypnotism and psychedelia to their singular strand of post-rock. The band of course were Quade, and the union proved to make perfect sense: Bruce excelled in gracefully fulfilling the band's vision, sealing their relationship for projects to come.

A couple years on, both Quade and Bruce had really proved the scope of their abilities: the sophomore album 'The Foel Tower' won the hearts of fans and critics across the board, who celebrated its "gorgeous" and "tender" sound to great acclaim. The world they had built clearly stood defined and dignified, though at the same time, Bruce couldn't help but wonder if there was more to be said. Besides, the sheer abundance of emotion and rich textures therein, suggested a great deal of potential for further exploring. So with the band’s blessing, he embarked on versioning the album.

Bruce was off the leash: total freedom leant him the ability to dub in wild style, weaving and wrestling with drum, bass et al, connecting to the arrangements' true feelings and expanding them to full frame. The "doomer sad boy, ambient-dub, folk, experimental post-rock" of the original, was blown into a whole new, hypnotic realm: through rattling analogue distortion and huge spaced out effects, Bruce's efforts stand as an exploding supernova of dub and noise, refracted through the band's themes of grief, beauty and the great British countryside.

A seminal, early highlight of shoegaze that helped birth the idea of “dream pop”, also serving as a blueprint of sorts for Dean Blunt's world of sound, A.R. Kane’s debut album is among the most under-sung, yet foundational, records of its time. 

A.R. Kane were no doubt an anomaly in their field - far as we know, the only Black band of musicians operating in British indie-pop-rock music - which only makes their dare-to-be-different style even more exceptional, in hindsight. They would famously go on to create a major touchstone of acid house and dance-pop with their über-classic ‘Pump Up The Volume’ as M/A/R/R/S, but before that they released debut album ’SIxty Nine’, laying out a template for psychedelic, grooving pop music that remains practically peerless in its field, with echoes of its sound heard everywhere from Micachu & The Shapes to Dean Blunt in the current day. 

After 32 years ’Sixty Nine’ remains a most beautiful sore thumbs-up, with tenderly fragile yet powerful vocals set to a mix of psychedelia, dub, jazz-funk, free jazz spirits and keeling amounts of guitar feedback, in a style that the band’s Alex Ayuli would describe as “dream-pop” - a term which has stuck and blossomed ever since. Mercifully, “dream-pop” provides a catchy phrase for their hard-to-place sound for clumsy writers like we, and is practically the only way to encompass their sound here; taking in the range of their jangling sorta Afrobeat/indie hybrid styles in ‘Crazy Blue’, thru to swooning dub-rock-pop of ‘Baby Milk Snatcher’, the charred guitar feedback scapes of ’Sulliday’, and the thizz of their spine-tracing vox, guitar, and hi-hats in ‘Spermwhale Trip’, alongside the chamber-like oddity of ‘The Madonna Is With Child.’ And considering that it was issued in a pivotal year for new music, it’s always worth listening to Simon Reynolds’ take, who sums up ’69’ very neatly in his review for Melody Maker as “the outstanding record of ’88.”

Seriously there’s nowt quite like this album. A 100% must check if you don’t already know.

items.body:
Following last year's long-overdue reissue of 'bloweyelashwish', Numero deepen the narrative with a new edition of Lovesliescrushing's prescient second album 'xuvetyn', compiled from hissy cassettes 4-tracked between 1991-'95 and a crucial stepping stone between shoegaze, tape music and power ambient -  essential biz if you're anywhere on the line from MBV to Jefre Cantu-Ledesma, Flying Saucer Attack to Windy & Carl.

We're still not sure how this one passed so many people by when it appeared first time around, way back in 1996. 'xuvetyn' is the duo's most perfect statement, a record that lacks the sheer shock of their debut but surpasses it elsewhere on almost every level. Producer Scott Cortez and vocalist Melissa Arpin-Duimstra assembled the album over a five year period, slowly collecting rudimentary experiments with a few pedals and a busted TASCAM Portastudio. And unlike its predecessor, it sounds as if it's been rounded out at the edges - still noisy, of course, characterised by tape fuzz and distortion that positions them somewhere between 'Loveless' and 'Endless Summer', but it flows seamlessly, foreshadowing the next few decades of euphoric, shoegaze-adjacent ambient gear. 

Without exaggeration, Lovesliescrushing just puzzled out a sweetspot between noise, minimalism, euphoria and repetition a little earlier than the rest. Inspired by Robert Fripp, Cocteau Twins, Eno, Jon Hassell, Glenn Branca and, of course, MBV, you can hear exactly how they absorbed all those influences, stretching Arpin-Duimstra's breathy vocal next to swelling, almost orchestral guitar drones. Stars of the Lid would get the flowers for their own response to many of the same influences a few years later, and - by the mid '00s - a more organic, shoegaze-aware brand of "ambient" began to seep into the underground's top levels: Fennesz, Tim Hecker, Jefre Cantu-Ledesma and others. The crazy thing is, so many of those artists' ideas were prototyped here; using 4-track tape tricks rather than granular effects or Max/MSP patches - Cortez and Arpin-Duimstra inadvertently mapped out a language that would define the laptop age. Just listen to the FM gamelan-cum-bleep techno experiment 'Virgin Blue-Eyed' and tell us they weren't years ahead of their time.

Prophetic, essential gear.

Jack Cooper and Tara Cunningham (1/2 of Modern Nature) present an LP as duo 'The Sleeves'.

"The Sleeves are the duo of Jack Cooper and Tara Cunningham, both likely known to you as one half of Modern Nature. Following an all-instrumental Mossy Tapes release last November, Cooper and Cunningham have recorded 10 new songs showcasing their vocal and guitar interplay with only the faintest echoes of prior efforts (individually or collectively), representing a fully realized leap forward from their largely improvised debut.

'The Sleeves' is a somewhat counter intuitive take on the guitar/vocal duo formula (provided you think there is such a thing) though it's not nearly as simplistic as "the space between the notes" - it would be the height of exaggeration to say an album this simultaneously expansive and incandescent is unprecedented. But it doesn't happen nearly often enough, either.

“What I initially found so familiar and exciting about playing guitar with Jack - and continually do - is that our approach to music is pretty much exactly the same. And that is - to celebrate the space that frames ideas, embraces silence, to play simply, simultaneously championing our respective unembellished guitar sounds, whilst looking for sounds that aren’t like a guitar at all - bells, birds, switching between radio stations etc. It’s rare to find someone who - whatever this means to you - ‘gets it’ - and I think when we started playing guitar together, we both knew the other had something of whatever our ‘it’ was.”

“‘The Sleeves’ is the sum of our shared musical journey thus far, an exciting mix of familiarity and uncharted territory in its approach to structure and how we use our guitars and voices. It feels to me like we are both citing shared references and traditions, whilst floating in our own, single-cell world that is completely genre-less. That grey area is where we seem to thrive. As Jack says, it feels like music that really couldn’t be made by anyone else.” - Tara Cunningham

“Tara and I started playing guitar together at the start of 2024. It was an improvised music night in a railway arch in South London. The set was great but there was a couple of minutes in particular where Tara and I really sort of locked in. We made a record a few weeks later. There was something in the way we played together that felt very intuitive from the start. We recognised a shared approach right away and an affinity to the way each other played.”

“During the summer we got stuck in a traffic jam coming home from a show in Glasgow. We spent a few hours singing along to the Mamas & The Papas and Simon & Garfunkel and over the course of the day, like magic we became The Sleeves. We're excited about it because it feels like music that really couldn’t be made by anyone else. We don’t bring different elements to it. We both bring exactly the same things. It’s the result of our similarities.” - Jack Cooper "

Following frontman Elias Rønnenfelt's indie throwback smash 'Speak Daggers', cult Danish band Iceage continue to shave down post-punk until it looks more like Britpop. RIYL Fontaines DC, Liars or Gilla Band.

It wouldn't be fair to say that Iceage divided its fanbase when they released the sleek 'Seek Shelter' back in 2021. The album was a surprise to their early champions who'd watched them move from noisy hardcore towards a Talking Heads-indebted post-punk sound, but it was also pretty universally acclaimed, its relative polish deemed acceptable because the songs were genuinely pretty catchy. 'For the Love of Grace & the Hereafter' arrives five years later and in the wake of Rønnenfelt's newfound notoriety - both as a solo star and a tabloid staple. So you can almost predict what direction the band have gone in; their sixth album is their most digestible yet, making its predecessor sound almost rough around the edges in comparison.

Rønnenfelt, for his part, actually sounds refreshed, his voice falling between Shane McGowan's and Bobby Gilespie's and for our money handling the pitchy oddball routine a lot more convincingly than Geese's Cameron Winter. But still, it's better suited to angular material like the Byrne-esque 'Match Head Girl' than it is to melodramatic indie-pop gear like 'No Fear' or Strokes-ish material like 'Tender Blades'. The album will probably be huge, it's just chewy like that - they should take Dean Blunt on tour with them.

items.body: Album reviews CAMiNOS Introduces Mediterranean-Focused Debut EP Angel Romero May 30, 2026 No Comments CAMiNOS Flamenco French music Mediterranean music world fusion world music CAMiNOS – CAMiNOS (Piment Rouge Production / ACEL WORLD WIDE / InOuïe Distribution, 2026) Marseille-based group CAMiNOS recently released its self-titled EP titled CAMiNOS (paths in Spanish). Led by composer and guitarist Germain Chaperon, the project presents original, inventive guitar compositions and a repertoire deeply grounded in Mediterranean traditions. CAMiNOS reflects a life journey, signified by the paths we follow, cross, and create. The EP features songs in Occitan, Spanish, and Italian. Musically, CAMiNOS skillfully amalgamates flamenco , jazz, contemporary music, and world music influences from India, Eastern Europe, North Africa, and South America. Chaperon’s guitar work gives the project a strong flamenco flavor. Vocalist Neda Cainero brings a passionate multilingual approach influenced by chanson, jazz, cumbia, reggae, and tarantella. Bassist Marek Eichler adds experience from the Czech and Dutch jazz-rock scenes, as well as later work with Gnawa music and flamenco. Drummer Sven Clerx contributes a background in experimental jazz and live performance. Together, the quartet has developed CAMiNOS as a finely crafted cross-cultural project that celebrates movement, encounter, and shared musical exchange. Author: Angel Romero Angel Romero y Ruiz has dedicated his life to musical exploration. His efforts included the creation of two online portals, worldmusiccentral.org and musicasdelmundo.com . In addition, Angel is the co-founder of the Transglobal World Music Chart , a panel of world music DJs and writers that celebrates global sounds. Furthermore, he delved into the record business, producing world music studio albums and compilations. His works have appeared on Alula Records, Ellipsis Arts, Indígena Records and Music of the World.

Olga Castro wrote the lyrical adaptation dedicated to El Salvador, while Samuel Ignacio Quirós Badillo composed the music. Alejandro Campos handled the arrangements and tropical instrumentation. items.body: 28 years after the wintry North, BJ Nilsen has released a surprise companion piece as Hazard. That’s a long time, but as one looks back, one gains perspective on earlier works. Winter is approaching in the Southern Hemisphere, which makes the release date fitting for these regions ~ even if these sounds of snow, ice and wind come from the Arctic north. The title, Pre-Lapsarian, refers to the time before the Fall of Humanity, when everything was innocent and pure. Regardless of one’s theology, it’s easy to hear the Arctic soundscape as pristine and undisturbed, even if to human ears it may sound forlorn and abandoned. A soft drone and cold wind launch the recording into the frigid air. Nilsen’s footsteps can be heard amid the quiet rustle, crunching into the snow. Louder sounds in the fourth minute suggest snapping trees and an approaching storm, and as soon as the danger is registered, the pitch of the wind rises. Many artists incorporate field recordings into their music or the other way around, but Nilsen is one of the masters. Allowing the natural sounds to dictate their counterparts, he creates passages that sound entirely organic, even when one knows they are not. Pre-Lapsarian conveys the stark beauty of the Arctic landscape while sculpting a sonic narrative: the distillation of a winter event. When the sound levels subside in the eighth minute, one feels as if one has survived a necessary foray outside one’s shelter and returned just in time. The weather remains frightful, but as the zipper to the tent is re-secured, the field recordist is again safe and sound. (Richard Allen) Available here

items.body: The sharp pluck of a Wayuu classical guitar opens “Cardón” before the bass drops and Afro-Caribbean percussions floods in. Ghetto Kumbé built the track around classical guitarist Henry Pimienta Pushaina and singer Lido Pimienta. Pushaina, a concert musician from Uribia, brings material from his Portafolio de Obras Wayuu para Guitarra, a project that translates ancestral Wayuu melodies to classical guitar. This pairs naturally with Lido Pimienta’s background; born in Barranquilla of mixed Afro-Colombian and Wayuu descent, she blends traditional rhythms like cumbia and bullerengue with synth-pop. Her high, clear vocal cuts straight through the percussion layers. The lyric she wrote with Ghetto Kumbé’s Edgardo Garcés follows someone standing in a river at night, cold water over their feet, their sins going downstream with the current, praying the moon holds the frost back till morning. The chorus keeps returning to “Solo deja que la brisa arrastre todo consigo”, let the breeze carry everything away with it, and Pimienta’s voice delivers it each time like the decision has already been made. Co-produced with London’s The Busy Twist, the Afro-Caribbean percussion drives underneath while the vocal stays above it. “Cardón” opens Cardones, the new Ghetto Kumbé album released on May 15, an eight-track record built around collaborations: Pimienta Pushaina also opens the album on “Wayakana”, while Nidia Gongora and Akilín appear on closing track “Belén”. In support of the LP, the Cardones Tour Europa 2026 runs through June and July, taking in Fusion Festival in Larz, Colours of Ostrava in Ostrava and Les Suds à Arles among the stops.   Stream “Cardón” HERE and get your copy of Cardones following THIS LINK. But tango allows for many fusions, ever since the 70s, and just as Kurt Weill fused opera with cabaret, this tango with alternative rock and Floydian airs flows naturally, especially because Manzanera knew what he was getting into.The tracks are linked, like a suite within the album. The guitar changes tones during the same long and sinuous solo, shifting from rock and ambient...to distorted jazz, until "Swimming," which wouldn't be out of place on Brian Eno's Before and After Scene, glides serenely with melodies that seem to belong to another world, which is definitely what Bible Black would do, making us not miss the 70s, because by turning the right way, everything is in the present; that's what the cover logo is about. items.body: Review by tszirmay — It's always a fine green morning (wink, nod) in ProgRogue Land when I get a message from Ally Carter, with a nice download for me to peruse. Because it invariably means a new album is about to be released from this talented band that I happen to admire since their debut. Their seventh album is the second volume of last year's tasty The Land, the Sea, the Air, which garnered rave reviews from yours truly as pretty much the majority of the Prog community. Ally, Tree, David and Tom are back once again, as if it was only yesterday , consolidating their musical stance on the degrading ecology of our tired planet. At the risk of repeating myself, this band sticks to its principles with orthodox zeal, maintaining not only their style and their immediately recognizable sound, but also keeping continuity with a personal artwork display that is applause worthy. Three mega tracks are their usual recipe, and why change that, after all they are not the Ramones! "Song of the Rainforest" will dominate 21 minutes and 21 seconds of your time, keeping you far away from those pesky cell phones, as well as all other modern technological distractions. Tree Stewart settles the proper mood on her perennially silky keyboards, stitching into the melodic fabric a sundry of effects, bassist Dave Greenaway laying down his basso profundo with meticulous authority, Tom Jackson ticking, tocking and otherwise locking, straight into the groove. Ally glides in with his jade green guitar unbothered , caressing his neck with one hand , while the other performs various wrist flickers on his six strings. The atmosphere is set, perhaps somewhere deep in the Colombian forest where it rains more than anywhere else, an ode to the mighty power that Mother Nature chooses to unleash willy nilly, at her discretion. When Ally interjects with his brassy saxophone, the instrument most resembling the human voice, he pleads the case for all mankind. When the blowing gets severe, it's surely a sign of repentance and begging for forgiveness. Heavy weather jazz time. The sweeping keyboards convey the sorrowful resignation of endless human intrusion into where it shouldn't belong, her ominously angry synthesizers (and famed Roli Seaboard) slash fiercely in defence of the despairing jungle and its right to survive, I daresay even flourish. Still heavy but not quite jazzy, more like organized bedlam. And then, extended peaceful interjections of velvety softness come across as soothing panacea, Tree's flutes leading the serene parade, ethereal yet very much alive. The crushing solemnity in the final section is heart stopping, Tree and Ally laying down a magic carpet ride of contemplative introspection, maybe even self healing, in essence. When the rhythm section forcefully slams its foot down, it serves as a defensive anchor being cast, a line in the forest that will not be invaded anymore, come hell or (gulp) high water! In my mind, and assuredly yours when you hear it, this is their finest track and finest hour ever. There is a reason why Tree Stewart was voted among the top keyboard players in prog recently, she can play like the wind, as witnessed by her immaculate display on piano on "Rivers of Tears", mastering not only technique but also impeccable emotion, as one can hear the rivers and the tears in her performance. Throw in the lush orchestrations, Ally's discreet guitar tremors, the subtle cymbal work, and the reverence in the bass, the only discovery left is Tree's vocal which is delivered with empathy. The swerve into a jazzier surroundings becomes obvious as the piano and sax conspire to whip up some well-deserved groovy frenzy, after all, these are consummate musicians! This 15-minute epic refuses to stick too long in any redundancy, so the mid-section suddenly flips the script by injecting more sombre sequences, led by a forcefully darker vocal chant, and then plummeting into complex rhythmic polyrhythmic chaos that will drop that jaw of yours. The churning keyboards swirl and twirl like dervishes on fire. Tree even daring a few 'space shanties' made famous by the late Gilly Smith of Gong. This section surely owes some winks toward that legendary band; there are many little hints one can discern. And just when you may think 'what could they possibly come up with next after such a two-handed slap across the musical face', the band opt for a swooning melody so immediately attractive that I fell to my knees hearing the first time, sung with utter conviction, as a cross between Olivia Sparnenn of Mostly Autumn and hint of Janis Joplin, I swear on my honour! Here, total simplicity rules, the orchestral keyboards convey harmony only a song title called "Paradise" could get away with. Indeed, this is most heavenly, even the sax plays the gentle card. Nearly 9 minutes of bliss that could have/should have/and would have continued for another 10 minutes, making my day and night. Wow! Their best yet. 5 seasons of Green

items.body: Review by Aussie-Byrd-Brother — Always a recurring home for titles and artists on the darker end of the Italian prog spectrum, Black Widow Records brings together theatrical doom metal band ExpiatoriA and established gothic/symphonic/dark RPI group Il Segno del Comando for a glum and evocative split album `Voci Notturne', inspired by an Italian TV series from 1995 of the same name. Working alongside each-other, the two acts have set out to recreate, in their own unique and individual styles, the eerie, cryptic and perplexing atmosphere of the show, and listeners essentially receive an EP's worth of new music from each of them.An aura of intrigue hovers over director Pupi Avati's broadcast and the subsequent distribution of the TV series `Voci Notturne' ("Nocturnal Voices" in English), considered a masterpiece of darkness and mystery. The ambiguous narrative weaves together politics, religion, history and the supernatural across continents and decades, with an unsettling atmosphere that grows as truth and illusion blur together. The fact that the series is not readily accessible in the modern era (outside of a heavily reworked and reedited version) has only enhanced its allure and reputation.Formed in Genoa in 1987, ExpiatoriA only released their debut album `Shadows' in 2022, with a live cassette following two years later. Taking the opening side here, the band offers a set of three murky doom metal dirges of branching passages and moods. Front and centre are vocalist AngeleX's pained vocals, moving between despairing wailing and slurred, guttural growling, and they envelope the band's sludgy riffing, mud-thick fuzzy bass rumbles and battering-ram drums with a suffocating and disorientating fervour. Spectral choirs, ghostly church organ and spoken word passages intensify the sombre ambience, but there are fleeting little glimpses of light and grandiosity.The flip-side comes from Il Segno del Comando, with over 30 years of standout modern dark RPI and gothic rock works to their name. Over the years, the group has constantly refined and altered their approach, moving between heavy underground rock and more overtly progressive rock arrangements (lots of vigorous and upfront keyboard soloing these days!). In contrast to ExpiatoriA's interpretations, ...Comando's pieces are more up-tempo, punchier and rockier, with many bombastic and stirring moments.Riccardo Morello's soulful commanding croon purrs throughout `Le due vie', where reflective reaching guitar strains kick in with a strident power, and no shortage of wavering Moog trills and glistening synths. `Il crittogramma' thrums with slinking electronics and runaway guitar-soloing, and `Litania per Emily e Giacomo' is a rousing and sophisticated ballad with elegant orchestration, making it the most overtly melodic moment of the album (a track that would actually be welcome on any RPI album). Closer `Egregoro' is a tasty instrumental of heavy guitars and plentiful synth soloing, contrasting reflective passages with ballsy hard-rock crunch, not unlike UK band Arena in parts. Infectious and addictive, what a powerful and memorable way to close the LP!Available on LP, CD and downloads, if you're one of those drawn to the shadowy corners occupied by darker Italian prog and unconventional metal acts, `Voci Notturne' just might be the temptation you need to fall for.Three and a half stars, rounded up to four for the Archives.

items.body: Review by A Crimson Mellotron — 'A Dramatic Turn of Events' is the eleventh full-length studio album from Dream Theater and theirfirst with then-new drummer Mike Mangini, who filled the spot for the leaving Mike Portnoy. To myunderstanding, the majority of the drum parts for this album had actually been written prior to thearrival of Mangini, and therefore, he does not get any songwriting credits. Nevertheless, thisrecord delivers the familiar sound of Dream Theater in spades, and despite a few moments ofexperimentation or play-around with other styles, many would safely call this a typical DT release.Compositionally, this is one of the strongest and most sophisticated works from the band, with themajority of the songs being rather lengthy, whereas the album itself bolsters a running time ofseventy-seven-plus minutes, which is a certain prerequisite for a demanding listen. I personallyenjoy this album every time I play it - the riffs sound really refreshing and the unbridledcomplexity of the instrumental sections genuinely blows my head off in a way that only Dream Theaterare able to achieve.Kicking off in a typical melodramatic fashion, we have the excellent song 'On the Backs of Angels',which sees Jordan Rudess playing a continuum in the intro section, and John Petrucci laying down oneof the most effective solos on the album. Apart from this, this song is by far one of the most"typical" Dream Theater compositions on here, which is definitely not a drawback, having become oneof their most well-known songs in recent years. Next up is 'Build Me Up, Break Me Down', a shortersong that instead tries to break away from the band's usual sound and introduces a crunchy nu-metalaesthetic, which is pretty interesting (given that the end result is really solid). The third albumtrack 'Lost Not Forgotten' is an intense piece of prog metal containing all the delightfully complextwists and turns one would expect from Rudess and Petrucci's writing, who would establish themselvesas the primary songwriters of the band for years to come. More melodic guitars enter the scene onthe following track 'This Is the Life', which among other things, slows down the album after thebombastic beginning. With the synth-laden prog rollercoaster 'Bridges in the Sky' and the anthemicsuite 'Outcry', Dream Theater mark a return to their epic sound, offering two lengthy songs thatimpress with some truly creative sections, very musical and ornately composed. The final tracks onthis record include the elegiac 'Far from Heaven', the theatrical epic 'Breaking All Illusions' anda decent pop song that closes off ADTOE.This album does not redefine the progressive metal genre, but in my view this was never the point ofit. It simply serves as an excellent example of songwriting mastery and in my ears happens to be oneof Dream Theater's most consistent efforts in the last fifteen years or so.

items.body: Review by A Crimson Mellotron — Having been listening to this album for years now, I still find the opening track 'The City Has NoEmpathy' the most interesting and memorable part of it. 'Scenes from Ephemeral City' is the 2011self-released debut studio album from Australian progressive rock/metal band Caligula's Horse, whowere founded by guitarist Sam Vallen (who is the engineer and producer of this release) and vocalistJim Grey sometime in 2010. The band's powerful and melodic style is quite impressive and immediate,as heard on this daring debut collection, which is also fairly accessible. Achieving a fine balancebetween the technical guitar-heavy parts and the dreamier melodic passages, C-Horse deliver arecognizable style that definitely emphasizes the warm and expressive singing style of Jim Grey, whois a truly excellent performer. 'Scenes' was definitely composed by guitar player Sam Vallen, whoexhibits a fabulous command of his instrument, including several crafty acoustic bits, a good amountof really technical, proggy riffs, and an abundance of musically acute solos.The music on this album resembles the output of Scale the Summit, Plini and Haken, all of which arecontemporaries of Caligula's Horse, and are often mentioned together in discussions on the new waveof prog metal. As for the album itself, the original track list features seven songs, of which theaforementioned opening track is a really strong contender for being one of the most memorable piecesof modern prog metal, with its gritty guitar playing and inviting vocals. The two instrumentals'Singularity' and 'Calliope's Son' are really good, too, but some of the longer tracks like 'Alonein the World' (sitting at eleven minutes) and 'Silence' (at seven) fail to leave a lastingimpression and miss that characteristic sound or hook that the band would deliver on subsequentreleases. The Inside Out Music reissue of this LP features two extra tracks, of which the single'Colossus' is a really fine entry and once again exhibits the inherent melodicism within Caligula'sHorse's songwriting. Overall, this is an impressive debut album, especially given the fact that itwas self-produced and self-released (it does sound great all the way through!), but it lacks notableideas, which makes it one of the least impressive corners of the band's discography.

items.body: Review by tszirmay — "Gil Gilad was formed in County Durham, UK, in 1979 by university students interested in long-form music. The original members went their separate ways sometime after 1981. Three of the original members (Paul Dobson, Kev Stevens, and Nev Tobin) started writing music again starting around 2015 when the band made its appearance with a Facebook page sharing tracks from Soundcloud. After many years, the band finally released its debut album in 2024 titled 'A Record of the Unworldly and the Strange' inspired by entrepreneur and chemist John Walker. The current line-up as of December 2025 is Paul Dobson (guitars, keyboards, backing vocals), Nev Tobin (lead vocals, keyboards), Kev Stevens (drums, keyboards, guitar, backing vocals), and Geoff Parkin (lead guitar, backing vocals)". This is the second chapter in the Walker saga, and as such, the band take us on a sweeping 70-minute sonic adventure, with nods and winks to a series of classic British writers as well as harkening back at classics like Jeff Wayne's War of the Worlds.HG Wells is the ignition for the opener "Prisoners of Time", a prototypical neo-prog track that features all the instrumentalists showing off their wares, blitzing synthesizer and keyboard runs, solid bass underfoot, concrete drum propellants and Nev Tobin's rather attractive vocal tone and delivery. 'We all have time machines?those that take us back are memories and those that carry us forward are dreams.'Up next under the auspices of philosopher, logician, mathematician Bertrand Russell "We Are Scientists Not Philosophers" selects a lighter approach to complex thought based on 'Science is what you know. Philosophy is what you don't know'. Here the tempo is first leisurely and playful, with a sudden plunge into darker spheres where the austere narration challenges the weakness of mind. The rhythmic piano is maddeningly efficient, as it sits front and center, its ivory keys glowing brightly. There is a definite art-rock slant, perhaps winking at bands like 10cc or even Alan Parsons Project. "The Traveller: Altered Destiny" has theoretical physicist Charles Peacock as an influence, and musically, the APP hint comes across luminously, swirling keyboard setting the foundation on which basic bass and drum stakes are planted 'We explore the vagaries of time; Parallel worlds where everything happens in tandem with everything else. However, our minds are ill-disposed to extract the truth behind the thin veils that blind us.' An exuberant electronic prog workout that offers a most attractive plane to enjoy, melodically powerful, yet accessible, full of thrilling spills. There is an 80s electro feel to the vocals which are extremely attractive, as it comes across well with all the backing mellotrons, a fascinating track to be sure! John Walker speaking of his loss of Hai-Yun is expressed on "A Chance to Speak" , a short two-minute waver, dispensing a very elegant British sound, focused on piano and aery vocals. 'I last saw her on the outskirts of Durham?How she danced on those silken, silver threads I will never know: She was elegance and strength, and light as floating feathers?'. A proggier trio of tracks form the middle core of this release, and my favourite section , first up "The Watchers", owner of a cinematic slice of imaginary sights and sounds, caught in a lush whirlwind, immediately attractive with a strong melodic spine and dramatic vocals that include amazing, hushed backing vocals and effects galore. 'The primary objective of a Watcher is to ensure the safety and security of the community, by whatever means necessary within the limits of the primary directive set out in Principles of Service'. This track could have ben a segue to APP's I Robot masterpiece "The Voice". Next of kin, "Escape from York" possesses a cosmic urgency that felt like running from the devil. Hurried, panting and awesome electronics make this cascading piece of energy most compelling. The looping bass finale a killer. 'We need to go, or you will not live out the hour!' . Who else but the perennial JRR Tolkien as inspiration on a Kate Bush-like vocal to die for on "A Walk in the Woods" (6:14), a stylistically dynamic tour de force, showing intense attention to mood and atmosphere, a comfortable sense of freedom of pace, even though engulfed in the mysterious solitude of nature. 'I thought all the trees were whispering to each other, passing news and plots along in an unintelligible language; and the branches swayed and groped without any wind.' The loving screech of Geoff Parkin's electric guitar does the piece justice. A definite highlight. A welcome return to "Dreams of Samira" channels a page from Percy Byshe Shelley's Love's Philosophy, recalling German band RPWL in terms of style and structure, keyboard and rhythm section heavy, sliced open by a bitter guitar recollection, weaving expertly with a companion synthesizer expression, piano and mellotron to finish off. 'Nothing in the world is single, All things by a law divine. In one spirit meet and mingle. Why not I with thine?'On the two next thrilling pieces, William Gibson the American-Canadian writer ("Neuromancer") provides the essence for the more experimental "The Burghers", a clanging glance into the impending fate of mankind, based on sociological conflicts that are now a global spectacle. Cyberpunk rebellion of yore now transforming itself into internet anarchy. 'The future has already arrived; it's just not evenly distributed yet'. Musically, it's a deliberate ball of confusing distortions, oblique settings and a desperately gloomy finale. "Before Today is Yesterday" suggests too many voices in our heads, forming a dangerously growing series of phenomena as insomnia, depression and data fatigue. No time left for yesterday's reality, only tomorrow's incertitude. Opinion-peddling rules the day. 'And we danced on the brink of an unknown future, to an echo from a vanished past'. Nev Tobin stars on the grim "Darkened Embers of Suspicion" has a slight Kashmir-ian aura (the Led Zep version , not the disputed region!), a brooding snarl of reflection, the result of the previous discussed tracks, focusing on endless negatives, eschewing whatever progressive good has been achieved on so many levels. Negativity sells. 'In the wastelands of memory, our past haunts us when all is dark and rested. We become robed in lost moments, and half remembered phrases that twist and torment'.The pleasantly lilting "The Strange Long Night" hides an underlying message of disbelief 'Believe what? That tomorrow night beneath the full moon, I'll sprout hair and fangs and eat people? It's bulls**t!'. The piece is somewhat dark, quirky and oblique, the way an odd lengthy evening may easily become. What better segue than the tempestuous fury of "The Storm", a six-minute+ tornado of sound with raging synths, howling gales of mellotron, booming bass curvatures and tectonic drum patterns that will stimulate the blood flow. 'Batten down and lock up! Sound the alarm! Storm coming!'. A relentless pummeling can do wonders for the energy levels, lest we forget that Mother Nature can be cruel to be kind, in the right measure. The 70-minute opus finalizes its run on "The Nature of Time", a hint from William Wordsworth's "Composed During a Storm", showing abundantly the painstaking details marshaled by the band in maintaining flow, thematically as well as infusing sufficient musical variety to keep the headphones on, all along the adventure. "He raised his eye Soul-smitten; for, that instant, did appear large space ('mid dreadful clouds) of purest sky, An azure disc, shield of Tranquillity; Invisible, unlooked-for, minister of providential goodness ever nigh!". A solitary two-note piano puts this to bed effortlessly.An excellent album, that caught me quite by surprise, as the first audition had not grabbed me completely. By the second, it was hook, line and sinker. Bravo, lads , well played! 4.5 whiskey sours.

items.body: Review by Finnforest — Another Mystifying Turn While 1989 saw the release of the wonderful archival Donna Plautilla, it also brought asecond release that year in the form of Non Mettere Le Dita Nel Naso. Google translates thisto "Don't Put Your Fingers in Your Nose," which sums up pretty well, unintentionally or perhapssubconsciously, how unnecessary this release actually was. Confusing labeling indicates both a Bancoalbum and a Francesco Di Giacomo solo album, almost as if the PR team involved couldn't figure outwhat it really was. After hearing the music, one can understand why.I will give them credit for keeping the songwriting in house. Other established pop/rock artistsbegan subbing out this most important part of their craft to paid "hitmakers." While that practicehad always happened for non-songwriter "performers," it is tragic when it becomes embraced by actualmusicians who have proven their songwriting skills already in the past, only to capitulate theirpersonal artistry to product movers due either to label pressure or lost artist confidence. The material here is sadly reminiscent to E Via, though not identical. It has perhaps morerange of styles, better arrangements, and just slightly longer tracks for elaboration. As always,the Banco musicians and the long roster of guests are fantastic players, and we are treated totalent and production quality that stands with anyone. However, as with E Via, the problem isthe material. Who are they making this record for? Despite the treasure they have in Di Giacomo'svoice, despite the finesse of all players involved, there is nothing here that is going to excitethe progressive rock fans of the Darwin era. There is nothing that excites me as a fan ofBuone Notizie's surprisingly fun concoction of mischief and chops. It has a few interesting performance and sound choices here and there. "Qualcosa che rimane" is thestandout moment showcasing Francesco in the spotlight with only very subtle and refined keyboardsand guitar as support. But even if the goal here was pop perfection, others do it better. Thesetracks are a bit long-winded and middle-of-the-road to capture the succinct sugar high pop fanscrave. What to even compare this to? Mid '80s Meatloaf, Celine Dion, a lesser Steve Winwood moment?Answer: It doesn't matter. The only thought I have while listening is pondering what else I could belistening to instead. There is a templated contrivance to the song structures which stranglesimmediacy---very "session-y" sounding instrumental leads laid atop an almost programmed-feeling,often generic backing.The music is not necessarily bad if you have a fetish for sophisticated, middle-aged empty-caloriegloss, and I again resist giving Banco the one-star treatment out of respect for these legendary RPImusicians. But I just can't recommend this album enthusiastically to anyone either. It doesn'tconnect with me in any way. It feels lost in terms of finding its own niche or even finding its ownnecessity. The apparent lack of direction at this point would be further evidenced two years laterwhen they would remake their first two classic albums. I can't get excited about that either. I haveno interest in hearing progressive rock icons attempt to re-conjure the magic of glorious youth,whether that is Banco or Roger Waters. So in my eyes, it does feel like Banco is now firmly lost inthe wilderness artistically. All that said, I also worry this overly harsh take may stem from my own myopic taste profiles, and Iadmit to being less certain about the rating than I was with E Via. Thus I hope others herewill double check me on this---listen to this album and review it. Am I missing the genius somehow?

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — An utterly unique band to emerge in Spain's late 70s prog scene, AZAHAR which was named after anorange blossom flower and really did bloom into its own unique cultivar of musical ingenuity thatcould be referred to as something like symphonic progressive space Rock Andaluz. This band was oneof the first progressive bands to emerge in 1976 after the collapse of the Franco regime anddelivered two extraordinary albums in its three year run before exiting the scene in 1979. Despiteits short run the band had a significantly different lineup on its two albums with only vocalistDick Zappala and guitarist Antonio Valls appearing on the two releases. On this debut ELIXIR whichcame out in 1977, keyboardist Gusatovo Ros and bassist Jorge Barrai filled the remaining slots.AZAHAR was a very rare breed in that it managed to release an entire album with no drummer to befound which is practically unheard of in any sort of rock music. Instead the primary rhythmicbackbone was delivered by the thumping bass grooves. An elegant album that featured seven distinct track that didn't quite reach the 38 minute mark,ELIXIR featured extremely lush and complex keyboard arrangements accompanied by catchy flamencoinfused melodies along with passionate vocals as well as driving rock guitar heft and heavy bassgrooves sounding something like an oddball mix of Triana, the French space rock act Pulsar, thepastoral folky aspects of Genesis along with knotty prog time signature workouts and unexpectedtransitions. Add to that beautiful Middle Eastern melodic touches all completely forged without theaid of a drummer. The extra emphasis is clearly on the rich layers of synthesizers, Fender Rhodesand mellotrons but the flamenco and rock guitar parts are very much in the forefront much of thetime as well. Very much in vein of the Rock Urbano that was underway, AZAHAR delivered passionateSpanish lyrics emulating the style of the Italian prog scene however the Andalusian flamenco kept itfirmly on Spanish territory.The opening "Campos de Azahar" ushers in the album with larger than life layers of keyboard swellswhich sets the tone for the space rock aspects of the album and it's not until well into the secondtrack "�Qu� malo hay, se�or juez?" that the rock guitar kicks in and then game on as the bandengages in one of those dialogue albums where the keys and guitar parts sound like their talking toeach other. The third track "�Es que esto no tiene nombre!" introduces a greater emphasis on moreangular progressive complexities time signatures run amok, hairpin turns into varying motifs and amost satisfying scorching acid rock soloing sequence that trades off with the keys in unique ways.In some ways it reminds me of what Symphony X would latch onto a couple decades down the road onlythis track is more like the ridiculously extreme crafty complex antics of bands like the ArgentineanAlas or Italian masters Museo Rosenbach. Some of the keyboards remind me of the French zeuhl actArcha�a when sustained oscillating high notes roar above it all.The balance between instrumental development and vocal led structured songs give the album abeautifully eclectic style as well as the dynamics shifting from more pastoral sensual folky motifsand then into crescendoing uproars of keys and guitars getting wild. Vocal aspects are diverse aswell with not only passionately delivered lyrics out of the Italian prog playbook but also findmoments of group harmonies. Extra touches from the mandolin and Middle Eastern rhythms weaved intothe flamenco and symphonic prog is beautifully performed. Other tracks such as "Mercaderes," "UnHombre Cansado" and "Cantaros de Fuego" continue the magic with the latter offering some of thecoolest bass lines in prog but the highlight may be the closing three part suit "Viaja a Marruecos"which wastes no time delivering the prog goods with an endless parade of variations throughsymphonic prog turf alternating with Spanish folk featuring Zappala's fluid vocal style. While nodrummer is one board a bit of exotic percussion actually finds its way onto this track offering someof the best excursions into Middle Eastern sounds. The band delivers on all pistons offering thisamazing climactic closer that ends in with a frenzied cyclical loop that ends the prog party well.I guess i'm on the opposite spin of most regarding this album considering how low its generallyrated but for my tastes this is one of my absolute favorite prog albums of the entire Spanish sceneand as far as Rock Andaluz bands go this band does it for me much more than Triana and other actsdue to the fact that this band had a creative edge unlike any other in Spain or anywhere for thatmatter. This album stands out as an utterly unique example of prog ingenuity nurtured in every waydelivering top notch melodies, brilliant arrangements and an even more impressive execution of itall. This album IMHO imbues the very essence of what Spanish prog was all about in the late 1970ssounding like all of the bands of the era rolled into one with the exception the jazz fusionists asthis album does not delve into jazz fueled frenzies however some of the most sophisticated progmoves do match that level of ingenuity. This is literally one of those albums i can listen torepeatedly and never tired of. Masterpiece in my book.

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — After a very eclectic debut that eschewed the typical Rock Andaluz playbook that was rockin' Spainin the latter half of the 1970s, the Madrid act AZAHAR followed "Elixir" two years later with itssecond album simply with an eponymous title and refined its sound to a more mainstream stylecourtesy of the addition of drummer Willy Rodriguez de Trujillo who hailed from Seville and honedhis chops with local bands such as Fly, Blizzard and Manantial. He replaced bassist Jorge Barral andsurprisingly the band didn't employ a new bassist for the part but rather used two sessionmusicians: Julio Blasco and Enrique Carmona to fill his shoes. Likewise keyboardist Gusatovo Ros(who left to form Azabache) was replaced by the less flamboyant Manolo Manrique so when the dustsettled it was really only vocalist Dick Zappala and guitarist Antonio Valls returning with acompletely different set of musicians around them.It's immediately apparent on the opening track "Expresso a Ketama" that the band shifted gearssignificantly by adopting the standard Rock Andaluz format of guitar, bass, keys and drums with thefocus on the flamenco rhythms in a standard rock format and deemphasizing the keys that were sodominant on the debut to more of an accent piece with piano runs, and more symphonic light elements.In this regard the band emulated the more pop infused bands such as Alameda or Triana, in a waysounding like something in between the two. While the debut fearlessly treaded in highly progressiveterrain, this second offering plays it safe which was usually the case with the late to the progparty Spanish scene with bands sowing their prog oats on the debut and then forced by financiallimitations to simplify their approach.The second track "La Naranja y el Lim�n" continues the simplified style and was released as a singleshowcasing the band's ability to craft beautiful flamenco infused pop hooks like the best of theSpanish bands. The album pretty much sticks to the new sanctified playbook alternating betweensomewhat faster paced tracks including the instrumental "Zahira" and the slower tracks with thelengthiest track "El Mago Acidote" serving as the best example at 9 1/2 minutes in playing time witha slow ballad-like demeanor yet salvaged by Zappala's passionate vocal delivery which showcases hisrange and creative singing style. The track "Aire y Fuego" offers some interesting syncopationoddities while retaining its flamenco rock sensibilities along with some of the Middle Easternflavors from the debut. The closing "Espresso de Ketama" closes with a another flamenco flavoredinstrumental with a bit more emphasis on the keyboards.Overall this is a major departure from the uninhibited creativity of the debut which for my tastesyielded one of the best progressive rock albums in all of Spain. This self-titled followup is muchmore streamlined for the marketplace and features a fairly uniform approach rather than theexcessive extravaganza of "Elixir." While i much prefer the crafty compositions of the debut, for amore commercial approach, AZAHAR did a really great job of suppressing their most uninhibited progartistry and kept in on the leash while fortifying their standard approach with many of the sameflavors only used more as accent sounds rather than the whole enchilada. While the debut ranks highin my world, this second album is still decent although in this more mainstream style i'd preferTriana, Alameda or even the super slick pop rock band Asfalto nevertheless this is a reallyenjoyable album when taking it at face value and leaving comparisons to the debut behind. This wasthe end of the road for AZAHAR despite 1979 being the peak year of prog releases emerging in Spain.

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — One of the most important underground innovators of the psychedelic years in the former Soviet Unionwas the Crimean born YURI MOROZOV (later settling in St Petersburg) who was a multidisciplinarymulti-instrumentalist, sound engineer and prolific composer having released well over 50 albums thattackled virtually every modern genre of the era. Completely banned by the Soviet authorities anddenied access to the state label Melodiya, MOROZOV took matters into his own hands by releasing hismusic through the clandestine "samizdat" tape-trading networks which of course were totally illegalbut provided the means for experimental artists who dabbled out of the confines of the strict Sovietcensorship to release their music to the greater public at large.While the USSR was way behind the curve as far as Western musical innovations were concerned,bootlegs still infiltrated beyond the Iron Curtain and influences were adopted. What was really rarethough was for an artist to successfully record in such abundance and release dozens of recordingsto the public all without the sanctity of the state. MOROZOV was not only one of the most prolificand successful of these artists but one of the most wildly experimental. In fact i've never heardanything from USSR that matches his wild excursions into total psychedelic escapism as MOROZOV's 70sreleases with this one, "Сон в красном тереме (Dream of the Red Chamber)" sitting as one of the mostuninhibited albums of all to emerge from the former USSR.This renowned tape recording that finally found a vinyl release in 2014 was recorded between 1973and 1976 although the official date by some is 1975. Apparently the original release featured lesstracks than the 2014 reissue and like all Soviet artifacts from the past, especially from the deepunderground remains a little murky in details but one thing is for sure and that is the fact MOROZOVtruly captured the spirit of the psychedelic 60s and took it all the way to the level of the mostkosmische trip out musical statements of the German Krautrock scene. This album is based on aconcept adopted from the Chinese novel called "Dream Of The Red Chamber" but the musical flow ismore akin to a psychological mind trip taking the most lysergic aspects of psychedelic rock to theirmost terrifying limits. MOROZOV was a master of overdubbing and sound manipulation, sort of theAchim Reichel of the USSR only with a bit of Daevid Allen's Gong thrown in for good measure.The album original featured two versions of the title track broken down into two parts. Highlyexperimental in nature, the music features psychedelic rock, Russian folk, progressive rock and lotsof the earliest examples of the Soviet electronic music scene. It's a shape shifting type of albumthat goes for the psychedelic jugular. Many will find this aimless and simply self-indulgent as it'sa really difficult album to follow. Is there any point to it at all? Well, who knows. It sounds veryimprovisational with little to latch onto as far as structured compositions are concerned howeverit's psychedelic after all and if the aim of the genre is to create an ethereal otherworldly effectwhere the status quo is blissfully ignored and replaced by a consciousness recalibration sessionthen this is indeed the ticket especially considering the time and place of its creation. It's verymuch a dream state kind of album and in that regard it's brilliant. While the musical motifs are very non-musical there are plenty of avant-garde excursions thatimplement patterns of some sort. It's like listening to alien music in that regard. MOROZOV hasoften been called the Soviet version of Sun Ra and that would be quite fitting indeed as thisrelease is very much like Sun Ra's most "out there" moments even if it's not rooted in jazz.Obviously not to everyone's tastes but for the moments when i really want to take a deep dive intoextremely surreal soundscapes and simple psych flavored pop just won't cut it, albums like this riseto the top of the ranks and for my liking this is pure genius in how it exemplifies the spectrum ofthe most underground sounds compiled into a menagerie of free form psychedelic through the 65 minuteplaying time that is available for sampling (forget finding a real copy!) A true underground Sovietclassic here!4.5 rounded down

items.body: Review by tszirmay — Dutch composer and multi-instrumentalist Ruud Dielen unleashes another thrilling album, progressing now into the upper echelons of quality prog, as this is a standout release that had me smiling all the way through. Ably assisted in the task, bassist Tim Ros and drummer Kike Paglia man the rhythm section with authority, introducing three vocalists into the process, Frank van der Borg and Jyoti Verhoeff on lead and backing while Ties van Diesen on backing duties. Harrie Knapen adds Hammond and piano, Thomas Zunk with theremin and mellotron and sax player Reg Parham completing the line-up. The progression is obvious from the first note, as the album unleashes a snarling five-part title track opus that revs on all cylinders like a well-oiled machine. All the ingredients are in place, from an extended electronic introduction that seems to float above the clouds , settling the sonic groundwork into a comfortable zone. The mighty mellotron shows its impeccable grandeur in creating the symphonic mood that it manages so well. On "Part 2: Carrying the Yoke", the arrangement opens up the throttle in a more conventional neo-prog setting, laden with sharper tones, coarse guitar interventions and bombastic keyboard sweeps that elevate the vocals, at times gentle and then more forceful. Veering into more fleecier realms, where ethereal vocalizations (Jyoti) rule the heavens, "Part 3: Into the Clouds" showcases Ruud playing a rolling fretless undertow that hits the mark, thumping drum attack, as the tempo increases into a fiery hurricane of interweaving sounds. The splendid lead guitar work portrays a diversity that oozes class. Another brief instrumental bridge only adds even more pace and drama to the entire opus, setting the stage for another swift turn into the unexpected. "Part 5: Chaotic Spell" swerves into more intricate signatures, a demanding almost Zappa-esque escapade with bold jazz-rock tendencies, a platform for some delirious saxophone ramblings (Parham) and lead guitar forays that exude utter confidence. The drums flutter with a maddening splurge that defies the norms, propelling this finale with resolved expertise. Well done! "If You Please" is an extended instrumental rocker, an opportunity for Ruud to exploit his talents on electric guitar, using a wide variety of tonal shifts, assorted pedals (including the much-beloved wah-wah pedal). At times, it felt like Hillage-era Gong mixed in with ZZ Top zaniness, perfectly egged on by a dynamic rhythmic engine. Well-dressed fish ! Brooding strings, a hint of theremin, distant organ and mellotron on "If I Only", setting the table for an ominously sombre vocal 'devoid of empathy', both pleading their case with measured conviction. The biting guitar snarl heightening the theatrics, both rhythm shavings and lead flickers, the manic percussive attitude pervasive and threatening. Another excellent slice of prog rock. Keeping the thrill vibrant, the tentacular keyboard display on "Whirlwinds & Maelstroms" does the trick, a piece where the mellotrons blaze, the extended Hammond organ eventually overtaking the mood with a thorough onslaught of gloomy thunder, enough room left for the acerbic guitar shards to cut hard and deep into the flesh. These boys know how to play. Masterclass effort. The finale "Everything Must Break to Grow- Part 2 Reprise" surprises once again, as the female vocals (Jyoti and Ties) take over rather brilliantly in a vaporous premise, with huge harmony backing vocals, a dreamy soundscape floating in psychedelic karma. This turns into a rockier variation that shows plenty of backbone, as if the Legendary Pink Dots were the reference point, mostly evident on the voice effected final section with hallucinogenic tendencies that cannot be overlooked. Effing splendid, if I say so myself! The entire project did not need to rely on any 'elements of hope' to succeed but rather was dependant on raw unadulterated talent, cohesion, inspiration and dedication to create interesting musical statements. The Glorious Wolf has truly arrived.4.5 Cosmic hunters

items.body: Starsign emerged in the 1990s and was driven by the German duo Oliver Teßmer and Matthias Blechschmidt. At the time, they released several EPs, along with an album that appeared in 2003. After that, things went quiet for more than two decades, but the duo revived the project a few years ago. Following several high-profile singles, they released “Silver Linings” earlier this year, featuring 10 tracks. The influences running through “Silver Linings” are quite diverse, yet they fit perfectly within the Electro-Pop genre. The songs move between quiet, floating pieces on the one hand and more danceable tracks on the other. Depeche Mode can occasionally be felt lurking around the corner, while other tracks seem inspired by Mesh. However, Starsign is by no means a copycat; rather, they have managed to blend these diverse elements into a smooth and enjoyable whole. Some songs are beautifully crafted and reveal subtle details in the production. Personally, I prefer their ‘heavier’ tracks, and although I do miss an undeniable standout hit on the album, “Silver Linings” still has a great deal to offer. (Rating:8).
